name: Subcision
lead: Subcision is a minor procedure in which a needle is inserted beneath the skin to release fibrous bands tethering a depressed scar, most often rolling acne scars. The term was coined in a 1995 paper describing a tri-beveled hypodermic needle introduced through a puncture [1][2].

Proponents say releasing the scar lets the skin rise and stimulates collagen. Studies include case series and small trials, and general reviews list it within multimodal acne scar treatment [3][4][5].

paras: Acne scars are classified as icepick, rolling and boxcar [1]. Rolling scars are broad with a wave-like pattern, and subcision targets those held down by tethering [8]. Wikipedia describes blood pooling beneath the released area, raising the scar over time, and notes subsequent laser, peels or microdermabrasion are sometimes used [8].

A 2005 report described technique and outcomes in 40 patients [9]. Reviews place subcision alongside microneedling, peels and lasers, often in combination [3][4][5][10][11]. Wikipedia reports effectiveness for glabellar lines is debatable [8].

Forum users on looksmax.org discuss subcision as an option for tethered scars, with some reporting improved skin texture; at least one thread presents a do-it-yourself approach [12][13]. Dermatology sources describe it as a clinician-performed procedure.

Registered trials compare subcision with or alone against CO2 laser, platelet-rich plasma, exosomes, suction, cannula versus needle technique, and other combinations [14][15][16][17], and cellulite studies exist [18][19].

lore.intro: Subcision is discussed on looksmax.org as a step for tethered atrophic scars, sometimes after other treatments [12][13].

claims.claim: Subcision works for tethered scars better than microneedling or laser.
claims.believers: Posters say it improved their skin texture and that laser or microneedling does little for tethered scars [12].
claims.experts: Reviews list subcision as one component of multimodal scar treatment tailored to scar type [4][5].

claims.claim: It can be done at home.
claims.believers: A forum guide presents a DIY approach [12].
claims.experts: Medical sources describe it as an in-office procedure performed by a clinician [2][13].

card.summary: Needle release of tethered rolling scars; a recognized clinic procedure with mostly small-study evidence.
card.note: Described in medical sources as clinician-performed; DIY guides circulate online.

quick.overview:
Subcision uses a needle under the skin to cut the bands holding down depressed, rolling scars so they can lift.

It appears in dermatology reviews as part of multimodal scar treatment and is studied in small trials.
quick.mechanism: Releasing tethering fibres and creating a pocket where blood collects and collagen forms, which raises the scar.
quick.risks: Procedure-specific risks are not detailed in the sources reviewed; forum DIY versions are discussed online while medical sources describe it as in-office.
